name: Iris Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Iris, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do second fix, which means the finishing carpentry once the walls are up: doors, frames, skirting, kitchens, stairs. At the moment I'm on a housing association estate on the edge of town, sixty homes for social rent, and I'm usually doing three or four houses a week. I start at half seven, set up my mitre saw in whichever front room I'm in, and work through a list. I love the moment a door swings shut and clicks without touching the frame.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being one of two women on a site of eighty people gets old, though it's better than it was. My knees are already talking to me at twenty-seven. And the snagging lists, where someone walks round with a clipboard picking at every gap in the caulk, can make a Friday very long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's sort of where we are now, I think. I use it a bit and it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in small ways and that's about it. I asked a chatbot once to help me write up a quote for a side job, a fitted wardrobe for a friend, and it did a decent job. I'd tell people that, and say it can't hang a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to keep the life I've built. Noor and I have a good rhythm, she teaches, I build, and we've got over a year of savings from my nan's inheritance plus what I've put away. Nothing in this picture touches that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Maybe I'd use the AI thing a bit more for quotes and pricing timber, the boring paperwork side. And I'd keep going to the women in trades meetup once a month, because that's where the real help comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly smug, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the small savings of time actually change on your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the snagging, if someone used it to sort the lists properly. Right now I get the same note three times from three people. If AI fixed that, I'd love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office staff at the housing association, maybe. If it does the routine stuff, it's their routine stuff it does first. But in this picture it's small, so probably they'd be fine too.

S0.say: I'd say AI is useful in small ways and that's about it. A chatbot helped me write a quote for a fitted wardrobe once, but it can't hang a door.
S0.think: It means she keeps the life she's built with her partner, who teaches. With over a year of savings from her nan's inheritance and her own saving, nothing in this picture touches her.
S0.do: Carries on as she is and uses AI a little more for quotes and timber pricing. Keeps going to the monthly women in trades meetup.
S0.quote: If AI fixed that, I'd love it.
S0.fieldNote: Iris is relaxed and practical about AI, using it for paperwork without much thought. Her support network is the women in trades group, not tools. She's quick to think about other workers, like admin staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. More real. I've already seen kitchens come flat-packed to the millimetre from a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine as long as it's fair. If factories make more of the joinery, the people on site need training and a say in how it rolls out. And I'd say housing associations should use any savings to build more homes, not pay bonuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think second fix shrinks a bit but doesn't vanish. Somebody still has to fit the thing in a crooked old wall. I'm average, though, and the really fast fitters will get the work first, so I'd want to be useful for something else as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the bigger firms did for a year, and once I saw what was working I'd learn it. Probably a course on the digital measuring kit they use for factory-made stairs, because if I can measure for the factory I'm still needed. I'd keep saving like normal and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but checking the news more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year. What would you be looking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the people who jumped in early actually got more work or just spent money on gadgets. I've seen lads buy a laser level that does everything and then use it as a paperweight. I like to see it working on someone else's site first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, you always wait, just do the course. And she'd be right, but I'd still wait a bit. She's watched AI marking tools come into her school and she's more relaxed than me about it.

S1.say: I'd say change is fine as long as it's fair, with training and a say for people on site. Housing associations should put any savings into more homes, not bonuses.
S1.think: Second fix shrinks but doesn't vanish, because someone still has to fit things into crooked walls. As an average fitter she'd want a second useful skill before the fastest fitters take the work.
S1.do: Watches the bigger firms for about a year, then takes a course on digital measuring for factory-made stairs. Keeps saving as normal.
S1.feel: Uneasy, checking the news more but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I've seen lads buy a laser level that does everything and then use it as a paperweight.
S1.fieldNote: Iris's steady streak shows plainly: she waits to see proof on someone else's site before acting. Her public line is about fairness and social housing, which fits her values. Her private view is that being average makes her vulnerable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. That's... that's everyone, isn't it? Not just us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to step in now, not after. Some kind of basic income, public ownership of some of this, whatever it takes so the people building homes aren't the ones thrown out first. I'd post that and I'd go to the protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened for the first time about money. Even with a year saved, if robots can fit a kitchen in two years, my whole trade goes, and Noor's job could go too. Two incomes gone at the same time is the bit that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, stop the eating out, cancel the holiday we'd booked for Portugal. I'd move as much as possible into savings and pay off the car. I'd join the union properly, which I've been meaning to do for years, and look at what jobs need a person in a room, like care work, and ask around about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the scaffold moving under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first bill you'd stop paying, or the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday, then my gym, then the new saw I've been eyeing. Funny, I'd already be thinking of the saw as a waste, because what's the point if a robot uses its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you like to wait and see. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. That's the thing, with two years there's nothing to wait for. I'd hate moving before it's proven, but I'd hate being caught out more.

S2.say: I'd say governments need to step in now with something like a basic income or public ownership, so the people building homes aren't the first thrown out. I'd post that and go to the protest.
S2.think: She'd be frightened about money for the first time, because even a year of savings doesn't last if her trade goes and her partner's job goes too. Two incomes disappearing together is what scares her.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, cancelling the Portugal holiday and eating out, and pays off the car. Joins the union properly and asks around about jobs that still need a person in the room, such as care work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the scaffold moving under her feet.
S2.quote: Funny, I'd already be thinking of the saw as a waste, because what's the point if a robot uses its own.
S2.fieldNote: Her usual habit of waiting disappears under a two-year deadline, and she says so herself. The household risk, with both her job and her partner's exposed, makes her more alarmed than her savings alone would suggest. Her politics turn more urgent here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That I can at least think about without my chest going tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get ready and the government needs a plan for retraining and income. I'd tell the women in trades group to start talking about it now, because we'll be forgotten otherwise. Women always get left at the back of these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to see who's doing well and copy them, which is how I like to work. I'd be thirty-two at the end. I'd want to be in a role where I'm checking the robots' work, not competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years I'd keep fitting and keep saving, then I'd train as a building inspector or a site quality person. Those jobs exist now, and someone has to sign off a house. I'd also use AI more each year, once I saw what my supervisor was using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good at spotting what's wrong, ask anyone who's had me on their snagging list. And if a robot fits a staircase, somebody still has to be legally responsible for it. At least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the 2028 one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it in my own order. Watch, then learn, then move. In the fast one I'd be scrambling, in this one I can still be me.

S3.say: I'd say there are five years to get ready and the government needs a plan for retraining and income. I'd get the women in trades group talking about it now so we aren't forgotten.
S3.think: Five years gives her time to see who's doing well and copy them, which is how she likes to work. At 32 she'd want to be checking robots' work, not competing with them.
S3.do: Keeps fitting and saving for a couple of years, then trains as a building inspector or site quality checker. Uses AI tools a bit more each year once she sees what her supervisor uses.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she can work with.
S3.quote: In the fast one I'd be scrambling, in this one I can still be me.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets Iris follow her preferred sequence of watching, learning, then moving. She sees inspection as a role where legal responsibility keeps a person in the loop. She keeps raising women being left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'll be thirty-seven. Maybe Noor and I will have kids by then, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to do it right: training paid for by the state, and the money robots save going back into public services. I'd keep saying it at every meeting. Ten years is long enough that politicians have no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years means I'd probably be okay personally. I'd watch, I'd move into inspection or something like it around year five, and I'd have savings. My worry would shift to what kind of world we'd be raising kids in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting for a few years and see how the early robot sites go. Then I'd train for inspection in the evenings, paid for by me if needed. I'd vote and campaign for a proper plan, and keep an eye on it rather than rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's room to breathe in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might push them later, if I'm honest. Not because of money, but because I'd want to know I've landed somewhere first. Noor would argue with me about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's my weakness. With ten years I could easily tell myself next year, next year. I'd have to set myself a date, like my thirtieth birthday.

S4.say: I'd say this is the chance to do it right, with state-paid training and robot savings going back into public services. Ten years is long enough that politicians have no excuse.
S4.think: Ten years probably means she'd be okay personally, moving into inspection around year five with savings behind her. Her worry would shift to the world she and her partner might raise children in.
S4.do: Keeps fitting for a few years while watching early robot sites, then trains for inspection in the evenings, paying herself if needed. Votes and campaigns for a proper plan.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but with room to breathe.
S4.quote: With ten years I could easily tell myself next year, next year.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she relaxes about herself and starts thinking about future children. She openly names her risk of waiting too long and plans to set herself a deadline. Her calls for public action stay constant.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both me and Noor would be hit at once with nowhere to stand. What would help is paid retraining that's actually open to people like me, and a basic income for the gap, so you're not choosing between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone asked us. Nobody on a building site gets asked what they think of any of this. I've built sixty homes for families who need them, and a robot would never know what that means to me.

headlineQuote: I've built sixty homes for families who need them, and a robot would never know what that means to me.
portrait: Iris Lopez is a 27-year-old second-fix carpenter on a social housing estate, living with her partner Noor, a teacher, with over a year of savings partly from an inheritance. She uses AI now and then for paperwork and likes to see things proven before she changes. Mild pictures leave her calm; the 2028 picture alarms her because both incomes could go at once. With more time she plans to move into building inspection, while pushing for public retraining and income support and worrying about the women left at the back.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her partner would both lose work at once with nowhere to stand.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining open to people like her and a basic income to cover the gap, so nobody has to choose between rent and learning.
